## Fundamentals of Supply Chain Management {#slide-30}

- Tasks, terms and concepts
- **Objectives & trade-offs**
- Costs & management

## Learning objectives {#learning-objectives-strategic-fit}

After this unit you will be able to …

- **structure** value creation processes and the key drivers of a supply chain,
- **explain** the terms responsiveness and efficiency,
- **contrast** the implied uncertainty of a market with the responsiveness of a supply chain,
- **assess** the strategic fit of a supply chain configuration.

**Further reading**

- **Strategic fit, supply chain drivers and implied uncertainty:** [@chopra2025supply, Chapters 2–3].
- **Matching supply with demand and operational capability:** [@cachon2024matching, Chapters 1–3].
- **Supply chain strategy and value-oriented logistics:** [@christopher2023logistics, Chapters 2–4].

## Value creation as a process {#slide-31}

![](images/clipboard-2707534972.png){width="1500"}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="69%"}
***Procurement*** is the process of purchasing and providing raw materials, components and services from external partners that are required for the production of goods and services.

***Production*** is a purposeful process of combining goods and services into higher-value products.

***Distribution*** covers the physical distribution of goods from the manufacturer to the end customer and includes warehousing, transport and logistics of finished products.

***Sales*** is the process of selling the end products to consumers or trading partners.
:::

:::: {.column width="30%"}

::::::

## Strategic manufacturing {#slide-33}

::: slide-subtitle
Thinking in cycles
:::

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}

**Customer order cycle**: processing of external customer demand

**Distribution/replenishment cycle**: conversion of customer demand into internal demand for finished products

**Production cycle**: conversion of internal demand into production requirements for intermediate products and raw materials

**Procurement cycle**: design of ordering/supply processes for raw materials and services that have to be sourced externally

::::

## Implied demand uncertainty

Uncertainty of the demand segment that the supply chain is intended to serve, based on the defined demand attributes
:::

## Dealing with uncertainty {#slide-37}

::: slide-subtitle
Customer needs & implied uncertainty
:::

| Customer needs | Causes implied uncertainty because ... |
|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| (Max.) demand quantities increase | Wider range of demand causes greater variance / fluctuation of demand quantities |
| Lead time decreases | Less time remains to react to demand fluctuations |
| Number of products offered increases | Demand for individual products is harder to forecast |
| Required service level increases | Demand peaks now have to be absorbed |
| Degree of innovation increases | Demand for new products is usually unknown or hard to forecast |
| Number of sales channels increases | Demand per sales channel is harder to forecast |

## Responsiveness

is the ability of a supply chain to deal with demand uncertainty
:::

::: vspace-2
:::

*Responsiveness can be achieved, among other things, through*:

::: {.small-text}
- High inventory levels
- Short response/lead times
- High product variety
- Short development cycles for new products
- High service levels
- Reduction of supply uncertainties
:::

## Efficiency

The efficiency of a supply chain is the inverse of the total costs of a supply chain, i.e. of all costs of a product from
:::

## Strategic management

::: slide-subtitle
Sub-strategies
:::

::: {.smaller-text}
|   | **Efficient supply chains** | **Responsive supply chains** |
|--------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Primary objective** | Meet demand at the lowest cost | Meet demand as quickly as possible |
| **Product design strategy** | Low product variety, focus on simple design and high throughput | Modular product development and postponement |
| **Pricing strategy** | Low prices and margins since customers are price-sensitive | Higher prices with higher margins, since customers are not very price-sensitive |
| **Manufacturing strategy** | High machine utilisation | Spare capacity to be able to expand production quantities at short notice |
| **Inventory strategy** | Minimise (safety) stocks | Build up safety stocks to buffer demand fluctuations |
| **Lead time strategy** | Reduce cycle times as long as costs do not increase | Reduce cycle times even if costs increase |
| **Procurement strategy** | Supplier selection based on cost and reliability | Supplier selection based on responsiveness, speed, flexibility and quality |

:::

## Strategic management {#slide-42}

::: slide-subtitle
Generic strategies & SCM
:::

::: vspace-2
:::

<!-- | Definition of strategy (according to Gabler Wirtschaftslexikon) | -->
<!-- |:-----------------------------------------------------------------------| -->
<!-- | Strategy is the fundamental, long-term behaviour (combination of measures) of the company and relevant sub-units towards their environment in order to achieve long-term objectives. | -->
::: {.small-text}

| **Generic strategy** | **Advantage** | **Basis of competition** | **Contribution of SCM** |
|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|:-----------------|
| Cost leader | Drive cost-efficient production | Lowest prices in the product category | Efficient, low-cost infrastructure |
| Innovation leader | Exploit market strength and deploy unique technology | Generate sought-after and innovative products | Secure short time-to-market, increase volume |
| Service leader | Tailor service consistently to customers | Meet customer-specific expectations | Enable customer-oriented development |
| Quality leader | Manufacture safe and reliable products | Unique product features | Reliable SC, quality assurance |
| Sustainability leader | Sustainable products and processes | Meet customers' sustainability expectations | CO2 neutrality, conservation of energy and resources |
:::
